summary:
Gorontalo stands under Indonesia's national framework: the revised penal code, the national security posture and the policing practice described below apply in the province, and the source inventory records no ordinance, raid, protection measure or support service specific to Gorontalo in either direction.

Indonesia does not expressly criminalise consensual same-sex activity between adults in private, but the penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and punishes consensual extra-marital sex with imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision effectively reaches consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The custodial maximum is given as two years in one source and one year in another.

Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protection and no hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors with no third-gender or X option.

Physical risk is rising nationwide. Vigilante mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia in a wave of 14 to 16 July 2026, including more than 15 trans women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage shared online. An October 2025 presidential decree lists 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy. A researcher documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Morality enforcement is sharpest in Aceh, where homosexuality is illegal under Sharia law and punishable by flogging or imprisonment, and in February 2025 two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship. South Sumatra also criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Provincial moral laws remain in force.

Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. A 2025 Pew survey found 93% of Indonesians rate homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'.
tangentialFactors:
The national security framing introduced by the October 2025 presidential decree places LGBTQ+ people alongside terrorism and separatism as a non-military threat, which reporting in August 2026 ties directly to a surge in vigilante attacks. Visitors should expect official hostility to be expressed as defence policy rather than as isolated prejudice.

Provincial variation matters across Indonesia: Aceh applies Sharia-based caning and flogging to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, while South Sumatra has its own criminalisation of same-sex conduct. Gorontalo's source inventory records no equivalent provincial ordinance, but national provisions apply regardless.

Public attitudes are documented as sharply negative: a 2025 Pew survey found 93% of Indonesians rate homosexuality 'morally unacceptable', and a researcher cited by The Diplomat records markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016. Social hostility should be assumed even where no specific legal barrier exists.

Indonesia's votes against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025 signal that protection machinery at the international level is not backed by the government.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition for Indonesian residents requires sex reassignment surgery and approval by a judge; Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors with no third-gender or X option on documents.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no hate-crime enhancement is available for bias-motivated violence.

The 2022 penal-code provision on extra-marital sex, in force since 2 January 2026, reaches cohabiting same-sex couples because same-sex marriage is not recognised; reporting indicates enforcement is selective rather than systematic.

Provincial moral laws, including Aceh's Sharia provisions, bind residents as well as visitors in the provinces where they are enacted.
outOfScopeNotes:
The custodial maximum under the 2022 penal-code extra-marital sex provision is unresolved across the source inventory: one source gives two years, another gives one year.

No source in the inventory addresses whether Gorontalo province has enacted its own moral or public-order ordinance, whether local police have conducted raids, or whether any local support organisation operates in the province; these remain not sourced rather than confirmed absent.

The status of the 2025 bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour is unresolved: it was under discussion in 2025 and the inventory does not record whether it has been enacted.
